subtopic: PEACEFUL PICKETING BY MEMBERS OF LABOUR UNIONS NOT TO BE DEEMED UNLAWFUL

speechtext:
Mr. C. G. MacNEIL (Vancouver North) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26, to amend the criminal code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the time at my disposal I shall merely explain briefly the nature of the proposed amendments. Section 87 of the criminal code deals with unlawful assembly, and as it is now, subsection 1 reads:
An unlawful assembly is an assembly of three or more persons who, with intent to carry out any common purpose, assemble in such a manner or so conduct themselves when assembled as to cause persons in the neighbourhood of such assembly to fear, on reasonable grounds, that the persons so assembled will disturb the peace tumultuously, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to disturb the peace tumultuously.
Subsection 2 reads:
Persons lawfully assembled may become an unlawful assembly if they conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner as would have made their assembling unlawful if they had assembled in that manner for that purpose.
I propose to amend section 87 by adding a proviso to the first subsection reading:
Provided such fear shall not be deemed to be caused on reasonable grounds if it be the result of peaceful picketing as defined in section five hundred and one of this act.
The purpose of the amendment is to provide that an assembly of trade union members engaged in peaceful picketing shall not be deemed an unlawful assembly within the meaning of this section. Immediately any reference is made to "peaceful picketing," it becomes apparent at once that there is necessity for a clearer definition of such action in the act. Accordingly I propose to insert the accompanying amendment to section 501 which deals with intimidation. The intimidation section (501) now reads:
Every one is guilty of an offence punishable, at the option of the accused, on indictment or on summary conviction before two justices and liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding

Criminal Code-Peaceful Picketing
one hundred dollars, or to three months' imprisonment with or without hard labour, who, wrongfully and without lawful authority, with a view to compel any other person to abstain from doing anything which he has a lawful right to do, or to do anything from which he has a lawful right to abstain,
(a)	uses violence to such other person, or his wife or children, or injures his property; or
(b)	intimidates such other person, or his wife or children, by threats of using violence to him, her or any of them, or of injuring his property; or
(c)	persistently follows such other person about from place to place; or
(d)	hides any tools, clothes or other property owned or used by such other person, or deprives him of, or hinders him in, the use thereof; or
(e)	with one or more other persons, follows such other person, in a disorderly manner, in or through any street or road; or
(f)	besets or watches the house or other place where such other person resides or works, or carries on business or happens to be; or
(g)	attending at or near or approaching to such house or other place as aforesaid, in order merely to obtain or communicate information, shall not be deemed a watching or besetting within the meaning of this section.
Here I should explain that the present paragraph (g) is in the nature of a proviso which is found in the Conspiracy and Protection of Property Act, 1875, which is an imperial statute. This proviso first appears in Canadian statutes in "An Act to amend the criminal law relating to violence, threats and molestation." chapter 37 of the statutes of 1836. It was reenacted in the revision of 1886, but was for some reason omitted when our criminal law was codified in 1892. In the period between 1892 and 1934 action was taken in some instances against strikers for picketing. In the case of The King v. Russell (Dominion Law Reports, 1920), Mr. Justice Cameron held:
The striker has no more justification for picketing than he obtains by the right of every British citizen to go about his own business in a peaceable way.
In 1934 the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), at the request of the Trades and Labour Congress, amended this section by adding paragraph (g), which followed the language of the Canadian act of 1876. He thus declared that it was the intention of parliament to protect by law peaceful picketing, although this term was not actually used in the wording of the amendment.
Although there can be no doubt as to the intention of parliament, the term in common usage is not expressly referred to in the section. This particular section has been difficult of interpretation, and consequently I propose an amendment which would repeal paragraph (g) in its present form and add as subsection 2 of the said section the following;
2. Peaceful picketing, that is attending at or near or approaching to such house or other place as aforesaid, in order merely to obtain or
communicate information, or to peacefully persuade any person to work or abstain from working, or to direct attention of others to grievances, shall not be deemed a watching or besetting within the meaning of subsection one of this section.
The advantages of this amendment will be readily apparent. It lifts paragraph (?) out from among clauses defining forms of intimidation and makes it more clearly a proviso in proper relation to the whole section. In this sense, it makes for better construction. The phrase "peaceful picketing" is introduced and defined very largely in the language of imperial and Canadian statutes. The words, "or to direct attention of others to grievances" are new, but deal frankly with the main purpose of peaceful picketing, and amplify the words, "to communicate information." If the law permits strikers on picket to communicate information to others, the additional words do not extend this permission substantially, but express the right in clearer language, and in accordance with common usage. The onus is not on the courts to interpret grievances, but only as to the manner in which such grievances are communicated to others.
Turning to section 87, so far as I can discover, it was never the intention that that section, dealing with unlawful assembly, should be applied to peaceful picketing. For that reason I would quote from Crankshaw's Annotated Criminal Code (1935) as to the origin of the section. Here it refers to the remarks of the royal commissioners upon the definition of an unlawful assembly. They are as follows:
The earliest definition of an unlawful assembly is in the year book, 21 Henry VII, 39. It would seem from it that the law was first adopted at a time when it was the practice for the gentry, who were on bad terms with each other, to go to market at the head of bands of armed retainers. It is obvious that no civilized government could permit this practice, the consequence of which was, at the time, that the assembled bands would probably fight, and certainly make peaceable people fear that they would fight. It was whilst the state of society was such as to render this a prevailing mischief that the earlier cases were decided; and consequently the duty of not provoking a breach of the peace has sometimes been so strongly laid down as almost to make it seem as if it was unlawful to take means to resist those who came to commit crimes. We have endeavoured in section 84 to enunciate the principles of the common law, although in declaring that an assembly may be unlawful if it causes persons in the neighbourhood to fear that it will needlessly and without reasonable occasion provoke others to disturb the peace tumultuously, we are declaring that which has not as yet been specifically decided in any particular case. The clause as to the defence of a man's house has been inserted because of a doubt expressed on the subject.

Criminal Code-Peaceful Picketing
There are a number of eases on record where police action has been taken against members of trade unions engaged in picketing in such a manner as to make them liable to prosecution under the section dealing with unlawful assembly. I desire to illustrate the point by reference to events which arose during the strike at Blubber Bay, British Columbia, last year.
A dispute arose during 1938 between the Pacific Lime Company of Blubber Bay and its employees. The members of the union employed every legal channel available to them in order to effect a settlement of the dispute. Conciliation and arbitration were conducted under the provisions of the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act of British Columbia. An arbitration board, under the chairmanship of Judge Macintosh, brought down a unanimous award. The award recommended the reinstatement of men who had been formerly black-listed because of union activities.
As a result of the failure of the company to give effect to the principal recommendation of the arbitration board, a strike was declared on June 2, 1938. The members of the union took all the usual steps to carry on the strike lawfully. One of these steps was to establish a picket line on the government wharf upon the arrival of passenger vessels at Blubber Bay. This picket line was maintained for months and cannot be described as anything but peaceful. The strikers would gather in a group on the wharf and simply carried placards which displayed the words "Strike on here " or, " Scabs keep away." On occasion they sang songs which were humorous parodies prepared for the occasion, but the general opinion was that they endeavoured by peaceful means to dissuade the strike-breakers, who were at that time being imported by the company from other points, from entering the employment of the company in order to break the strike. So far as I am aware, no evidence was shown that there was intimidation or threat of personal violence up to the final incident to which I am going to refer. Intimidation was not at any time charged in our courts so far as I am aware. There was no attempt to molest the imported strike-breakers as they went to and from their duties in the company's plant. No attempt was made to interfere with the operations of the plant.
Upon the outbreak of the strike a detachment of provincial police was dispatched to Blubber Bay. At first these police officers did nothing but protect property and maintain law and order in that community. Eventually, however, they were influenced by the company's officials and commenced to display a very unfriendly attitude towards the strikers.

With the exception of one or two incidents which provoked some disorder, the men on picket duty were at the outset regarded by the authorities as maintaining a peaceful attitude. Finally, though, it became apparent that the police officers were determined to disperse the pickets. Evidence was given at the ensuing trials that such intention was declared in advance of the evening of September 17, 1938, and the detachment had been strengthened accordingly. I think I may safely claim that immediately prior to that date the activities of the police were directed not so much to the maintenance of law and order as to the suppression of the strike and the dispersal of those in the picket line. This attitude was revealed in several ways. The officer in charge recruited strike-breakers from among the relief recipients in the adjoining district. The police did not hesitate to make it known by their language and actions that they were unfriendly to the strikers. They encouraged company employees to congregate on the opposite side of the wharf and at the same time that the strikers were on picket, with the resultant exchange of provocative language. Thereupon the police would peremptorily order the strikers about. As this picket line had been maintained for months, I submit it could not be regarded as being lawful at one time and unlawful later.
On the night of September 17, 1938, the pickets assembled at the usual time, upon arrival of the steamship. They were herded into one corner of the dock. With encouragement from the police, strike-breakers made an obvious attempt to provoke disorder among the strikers on picket duty.
The police officer in charge ordered the dock cleared. As soon as he gave the order, tear-gas bombs were used. The strikers, in obeying the order, and upon leaving the dock, were ambushed by strike-breakers, who had been furnished with white arm-bands to distinguish them. The strikers, in attempting to escape, were stoned. This resulted in some disorder.
About 2 a.m. the following morning, the police attempted a round-up of all the strikers who had been present on the dock the previous evening, and arrested them under the charge of unlawful assembly. Some later, of course, were charged with rioting, as a result of this stoning episode to which I have referred. One man was awakened from his sleep in his home, placed in custody, and later taken outside the room used as a police cell and brutally beaten up by one of the provincial police officers, a man who had been formerly in charge, and that officer was subsequently convicted for this offence and sentenced to six months in prison.

Criminal Code-Peaceful Picketing
That, I think, illustrates the attitude of the police officers on duty at that point. His victim was charged with unlawful assembly; he lay in hospital for many weeks, and is still.
I understand, in a seriously impaired state of health.
As a result of this episode, twelve men were sentenced for unlawful assembly. I knew them as decent, industrious citizens. They were not of the stuff from which criminals are made. Nevertheless they were made criminals under this section, because under the interpretation of the section the police found an opportunity to abuse the law.
I consider it a serious tragedy that men should be sentenced under these circumstances. They were sentenced to terms ranging from six to eight months.
The background of this struggle should be taken into consideration, particularly because of the interpretation given the law. May I stress this point. This isolated community was divided completely into two camps: one, comprised of the strikers and their sym-,. .*-uizers; the other comprised of those who were determined to break the strike. That is important when one comes to consider the manner in which the evidence was given. Another important point to note is .that strike-breakers, who were also members of the same assembly alleged to be unlawful, were not charged with being members of an unlawful assembly. Information was not laid by officers of the crown but was subsequently laid by representatives of the union, and when the accused, charged in our courts, were acquitted. Apparently it is not a crime to take part in what is alleged to be an unlawful assembly if one happens to be a strike-breaker, although it is clearly shown that some of these men participated in and were guilty of riotous and tumultuous action. I am convinced that no man would be behind the bars as a result of these events had there been levelheaded and experienced officers in charge. The trial judge carefully summed up before the cases were referred to the jury. He made it clear that it was necessary to establish in evidence three points in order to prove rhe crime of unlawful assembly: 1. There must be three or more in the assembly. 2. There should be a common purpose, whether lawful or unlawful being quite irrelevant. 3. The assembly must be of such a kind as to cause fear in the minds of those in the neighbourhood that the peace will be disturbed tumultuously.
On the first point, it was conceded in these trials that there were three or more, and that there was a common purpose, namely, to picket peacefully; and a legal assembly became 71492-239
an unlawful assembly only by the action of strike-breakers, aided and abetted by the police. The third point, a most important one, could be established only on the evidence of police officers and those in the neighbourhood, who were obviously biased against the strikers. There was a suspicious uniformity about the evidence given by these witnesses. Actually the men were convicted on an estimate of the degree of fear existing in the minds of those who were known to be prejudiced against the accused.

speechtext:
The criminal code. I am asking for a proviso to the section dealing with unlawful assembly, whereby trade union members peacefully picketing, not indulging in intimidation or threatening personal violence, shall not be deemed to be an unlawful assembly.
I followed the evidence closely, and at no time was it shown beyond reasonable doubt that property or lives were threatened. Bad feeling existed between the conflicting groups, but this was to be expected after a prolonged dispute aggravated considerably by the attitude of the police. As a result of my experience with these trials, and from the reading of cases heard in other courts, I am convinced that the law should be amended so as to make it clear that peaceful picketing should not be regarded in any sense as an unlawful assembly. May I also point out that such a proviso in the act would have a useful effect on the public mind and on the general attitude of trade union members and others towards this particular phase of strike activity.
With regard to my amendment to section 501 I shall have to state merely that the jurisprudence in this matter is very much confused. Even a casual study of the precedents frequently quoted by judges with regard to the interpretation of section 501 will show that they are contradictory. In almost every important trial reported, the judge has made his point by reference to precedents existing in common law or case law. There is confusion in the various provinces and contracdic-tion in the decisions given as between provinces.
I have not sufficient time to deal with the matter to-night except to point out that in a number of cases, as in the well known case of Rex v. Richard & Woolridge, heard in British Columbia, it was clearly proved that there was no molestation. In the case I have mentioned, the union notified the Edison theatre that they would strike. The men



Criminal Code-Peaceful Picketing
were simply walking in pairs on the sidewalk, displaying slogans inscribed on their raincoats. Unfortunately, however, they were convicted under section 501 notwithstanding that they were clearly engaged in peaceful picketing. There were also convictions in the city of Hamilton where, again, it was clearly shown in evidence that the men had merely walked up and down in pairs in front of the theatre, displaying signs. Other judges refused to grant a continuance of interim injunctions because they held contrary views.
I submit that this section needs clarification in view of the contradictory decisions that have been rendered, and for this reason the situation is most unsatisfactory. Certainly the law should be made quite clear in this matter. The trade unions should know exactly what, under the law, is permitted, with regard to picketing, and there should be no doubt as to the interpretation of the law in any court.
I do not intend to add to the difficulties of the courts; rather, my amendment would make it easier for the courts, in the light of the experience derived from cases heard since 1934, to deal fairly with charges in this regard. I understand that it is our procedure, when we have gained a certain degree of experience in these matters, to codify that experience in law. I submit that we have reached a point where the law in this regard should be codified. I may add that since this bill appeared on the order paper, I have received wide-spread endorsation from trade unions and trade union councils, and the approval of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.

The minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations:-
(c) providing the manner in which the average price of each grade of wheat shall be ascertained by the minister.

speechtext: Yes.

I think the hon. member who proposes the amendment has not taken into consideration the fact that in these sections we are not dealing at all with individuals in determining either the amount of yield or the average price. It is not the price which a man happened to get for his crop, it is the price he could have got for it. We are not going to be able to follow every individual round to find the price at which he sold his crop on a certain day, nor are we going to be able to visit every man's farm

Prairie Farm Assistance
to find out what particular quality of grain he had. But those of us who have farmed in western Canada know this, that, generally speaking, if you have rust in an area which reduces the grade of your grain, it probably reduces the grade of everyone's grain in the township, and perhaps in many townships.
If you have frost, the same thing happens.
If you have drought, the same thing happens.
If the quality of your grain is down because of any of these things, then the quality is down pretty generally throughout the whole area and to everyone in it, and that is the determining fact in this matter. It is not a case of whether this man has No. 1, that man has No. 2, and another man has No. 6, but we say that in an area where these crops are light, and they are light because of one: of these reasons of which I have been speaking, in all probability most of the people will have approximately the same grade. If it is all low-grade, it will be down round No. 4, No. 5 or No. 6; if it is all high grade, it will be No. 1, No. 2, or No. 3; but to go out and find what every man's grade of gram is, and pay accordingly, would be a very difficult,
I think an impossible, task. To start to figure out the different ranges of price in accordance with the amendment would be an impossible undertaking.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: I should like to point out. too, that it would be most unusual that No 6 grade would yield 50 per cent more than would No. 1 grade in the same district. subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT

very well, that what we should be doing was feeding wheat to hogs and we would be getting $1.20 a bushel for it instead of 60 cents. subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT

arrive at the average yield of the cultivated land in the areas? What kind of staff will be set up, and how far will he use the municipalities to get the information?

As an example of how inequitable this would be, I want to mention what happened in Alberta last year. In order that the province might qualify under the federal drought relief legislation, the area had to be one with an average of five bushels to the acre or less. I have here a copy of a letter sent to the minister by the minister of health of Alberta, which shows that in thirty-six municipalities the yield averaged from five bushels to seven bushels, but the grade of that wheat in twenty-eight out of the thirty-six cases was No. 4. So we find that the municipalities which had a yield of seven bushels with a grade of No. 4 were considerably worse off so far as monetary reward is concerned than those municipalities which had five bushels to the acre of No. 1; yet the department refused to accept the former municipalities because they had seven bushels to the acre, although, as I have said, they were worse off than those which had five bushels of No. 1. When you base your acceptance of an area on yield alone without taking grade into conside-ation, you are causing a great injustice.
Prairie Farm Assistance

It is all very well to say that you can feed low grade grain, but that is not always possible. Farmers have incurred certain obligations. The thresherman demands payment of his bill, the mortgage company wants its interest, the storekeeper expects payment of his account. These people are not going to wait until hogs are fed and disposed of. So this grain has to be sold. Therefore this section does create a great injustice, and I believe the amendment would be well worth considering. It would be far more equitable, and it would work just as well upon a township basis as upon an individual basis.

the fact I stated a few moments ago. Usually rusted or frozen grain provides a very good feed, and this legislation is assuring the people of the possibility of getting through a year when they otherwise would not be able to maintain themselves from anything that can be produced on the farm. With a fairly good crop of feed of any kind it is generally possible to get by one or probably two difficult years. We have not thought it wise to take years when there is feed into consideration in connection with the crop failure year, although I would call attention to this fact, that we have not omitted such difficulties as are created by frost or rust in considering the factors contributing to emergency as reasons for accepting the year as a difficult year. These may be some of the reasons for placing the emergency year in that column.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT
speechtext: But is it not rather a question of value? What difference does it make to the- farmer whether he has a larger quantity of frosted grain, or a smaller quantity of No. 1 northern? In the final analysis what counts is the return he gets from his crop, and whether he gets it from a smaller quantity of No. 1 northern or from a larger quantity of frosted grain should have no bearing on the treatment we mete out to individual farmers. I repeat, it is a question not of quantity but rather of value. Even though he might have a large amount of feed, if it is not worth more than a smaller quantity of No. 1 northern, why should he have to contribute a proportion of his production to pay another farmer who gets an equal return, so far as actual value is concerned? In order to be fair to all concerned, the question of value as well as the question of return should be taken into consideration. At any rate, the argument from the point of view of actual return should be given some weight in the matter.

subtopic: PERCENTAGE DEDUCTION FROM GRAINS MARKETED IN SPRING WHEAT AREA-PROVISION FOR ACREAGE PAYMENT

Speaking to the point of order, I believe an important question is involved in deciding this point of order. It
must be noted, for instance, that paragraph 556 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms is as follows:
The house can make amendments which diminish the amount of reduction of taxation, or postpone the day when the reduction takes place, although the amendments may increase to that extent the charges proposed to be levied upon the people.
So long as an existing tax is not increased, any modification of the proposed reduction may be introduced in the committee on the bill, and is regarded as a question, not for increasing the charge upon the people 'but for determining to what extent such charge shall be reduced.
I say that this point of order might establish a precedent about something for which as yet there is no precedent in this parliament, or perhaps even in the history of parliaments. At the moment we are not dealing with a matter of taxation. I would point out that we are dealing with a levy, which is something entirely different from a tax. There is no question whatever of increasing the tax burden upon the people of the country, because the country is not being called upon to supply any fund, except in the form of an advance,, or as a loan which is repayable.
Therefore the point of order cannot be considered to be on an increase of taxation, because in fact there is no taxation under this measure. We deal only with a levy. I cannot recall a precedent for this type of legislation, which introduces the principle of a levy instead of a tax. Therefore I say paragraph 556 cannot apply because we are dealing not with a tax, but with a levy.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE

speechtext: Righ Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) (for the Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before your honour leaves the chair, I wish to address the house for a very few minutes on a matter which I consider to be of the utmost importance. It is one which I have tried to bring to the attention of the house on several occasions since May 1. by questions addressed to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). His answers to these questions were entirely unsatisfactory, and the conditions which I then sought to bring to the attention of the house still prevail, only in a more aggravated form. I refer to the plight of the single unemployed.
On May 1 the provincial governments stopped all assistance to the single unemployed, and most of the municipalities also stopped giving them assistance. To make matters worse, charitable institutions which had been to some extent looking after this class of unemployed by supplying food and beds also stopped giving assistance.
When I was working on the farm, when spring arrived and there was sufficient grass,

Single Homeless Unemployed
we used to turn the young animals out to forage for themselves, but we never did so until there was sufficient feed for them to maintain themselves.
When the first of May came this year, it did not mean that there was any more employment than there was on the last day of April, and by no possibility could these single homeless men find jobs by which to maintain themselves. They were just as much in need of assistance then as before. Despite their efforts since to find employment they are still in the same need they were in during most of last winter.
Almost every city in Canada has its quota of these single homeless unemployed men. In some parts of Canada the municipal authorities are looking after them, but, of necessity, on a very low scale. Most of the municipalities in Canada to-day are almost bankrupt and are not in a position to provide for these men. There are in the city of Ottawa more than one hundred men who, since May 1, have had no place to sleep and who are entirely dependent for their food upon the charity of well-disposed citizens. I think it is the duty of the government to provide sustenance for these homeless unemployed until such time as work can be found. It is heartless and inhuman to turn them out on the street when they have no means by which they can get food and shelter.
When I brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Labour, he suggested that they should go to the employment bureau, and stated that a number of men had already received work by applying at these bureaux. I have now ascertained that almost all these men are registered at the employment bureau. The work which some men have found is of no value to the men who did not find work and who are still in need of food and clothing and shelter. I have before me the Ottawa Journal of May 5 with the heading "Police called to eject jobless." It states that when more than eighty members of the Ottawa single unemployed men's association refused on Thursday to leave the office of the employment service of Canada on Queen street without getting work, city police were called in to eject them. Surely we have come to a sorry pass when the employment bureaux have to call in the police to eject men who have made application for work and for whom no work is available. The position of these men is that they have no homes, no place where they can find shelter, and if they are not allowed to stay in the employment bureau they have to be out on the street. Since May 1, they have been living in a hall in which there are no
beds. If they sleep at all, and they must, they sleep sitting in chairs. I do not think that is good enough.
It is particularly appropriate that at this time the government should be not only just but should be generous to these men. We are getting ready to receive Their Majesties, our King and Queen. We are decorating and beautifying our cities and our streets for that purpose. But we are doing nothing and, indeed, less than nothing to improve the conditions of these subjects of his majesty to enable them to welcome him when he comes. Indeed, all the decorations and all the pomp and splendour in the city at the present time can mean to these men nothing but more heart-burning and bitterness because they can have no part in it. Last Sunday evening I saw them marching to church. It was certainly a sad spectacle to watch them marching along the street in their rags, the same clothes they have been wearing and sleeping in ever since last fall. All this decorating and show are surely a shallow sham while we allow men to starve and to go in rags in our midst, while on every side we see wealth and abundance. I urge upon the government that, merely as a patriotic gesture, if for no better motive, the Department of Labour should get in touch with the provincial governments and offer to come to some arrangements by which unemployed men and women too can be fed and housed and clothed at least during the period their majesties are here. It is just possible that, after that, the summer being further advanced, some work may be available.
The conditions which prevail in Ottawa are pretty much the same all over the dominion. I have a clipping from the Halifax Herald of May 3 which states that relief costs in Halifax for the weekly period ending April 28 are greater than for the corresponding period last year.
I take up the Vancouver Province and I find a similar story. The heading reads:
Warns job seekers not to come here.
That is, to Vancouver. The item is as follows:
A warning to unemployed men in neighbouring provinces not to be "misled" by stories of trade expansion in British Columbia has been made by J. H. McVety, general superintendent of the employment service of Canada. "It has come to our notice," said Mr. McVety this morning, "that a number of young men are drifting out here from other provinces because they have been told of a shortage of labour in B.C.
"Such talk is quite misleading. There is an
ample supply of men and women in the province just now to take care of all labour requirements."

Single Homeless Unemployed,
Indeed, the last report issued by the labour department in British Columbia, at the end of April, was that there were at that time on relief 74,000 men, women and dependents. I suggest that at this time, if merely as a patriotic gesture because of the occasion, we should try to do something for these men. I warn the government that the situation is serious. They are making beggars of these men, if not worse. The latest figures issued by the bureau of statistics with regard to unemployment in Canada, namely those of February this year, estimate the number of unemployed as 491,000. That is an increase of 6,000 over January, the date of the previous monthly report.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Can the hon. member say how that compares with February of last year?

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I have not the comparisons with me, but the number is greater than last year and the year before, and pretty much the same as in 1936.

Has the hon. member a
record for other countries as well?

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I am not concerned with other countries. Let the people in other countries look after their own affairs. We should look after ours.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: I should like to see that on record; that is all.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Anyone who wants to find out the conditions in other countries can do so by reading the public press and reports from various sources. We cannot evade this issue by saying that things are bad in other countries. That may be true, yet other countries may not have the surpluses of wheat, butter, fish and other commodities which we have. And while we have these surpluses, which an hon. member last night suggested we should supply to the needy people of other countries, we should at least use a part to feed people who are here, who are dependent upon us, and who to a large extent helped to produce these surpluses.
I sincerely hope the government will not disregard this plea, but will make an early and earnest effort to deal with the situation, by making provision for these men now so that they may, when work again is available, take their place as active producers.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Before we leave this question, I am going to make a suggestion, very briefly, and it is this. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maelnnis) has mentioned the condition of the unemployed men and has suggested that some-

thing should be done for them during the royal visit. I should like to make this suggestion to the government. Throughout Canada there are a large number of families, including children, who will be interested in the royal visit. Many of the parents of these children are on relief, and I was going to suggest to the government that a fitting way of celebrating the coming of their majesties to this country would be to get into contact with the provinces and the municipalities with a view to giving these families some additional assistance during the time their majesties are passing through the districts where relief people live. We know that a large number of these families will be going to adjacent cities where stops are made by the royal train, and on these occasions it is necessary for the parents to take sandwiches and other food, to make some provision for the children. I recollect that in the old days when I was a boy in the old country at the time of the diamond jubilee of Queen Victoria and at the coronation of His Majesty King Edward VII, the children of the land were given a special treat to celebrate the occasion. It seems to me that with so much poverty and misery and with such a shortage of things which the children like, our Canadian children would appreciate something being done for them by the various governments to mark the coming of the king and queen.

maintopic: SINGLE HOMELESS UNEMPLOYED-STATEMENT OF MR. MACINNIS ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF JUSTICE
speechtext: Since it is nearly eleven o'clock I would ask the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) if he does not think it possible that these children might squander that allowance, as was declared by the relief administrator of Alberta with reference to the fifty cents given at Christmas?

I do not think there is much danger of that.

As this is the first occasion on which we are going into the estimates of the Minister of Fisheries this year, it might be appropriate to spend a minute or two at least in paying tribute to his deputy who has left the department since the last session.
Doctor Found served the government for forty years, beginning as a junior clerk and working his way up by his own ability and by devotion to his duties. He had a long and distinguished career-distinguished at least by

Supply-Fisheries
*constant attention to his duties and a record of creditable achievements. Doctor Found was, above all, a worker, and he was always at his desk, holiday or no holiday. He practically lived for the work in which he was *engaged. He was the prime mover in negotiating the halibut treaty with the United States, and was for a number of years a member of the board under that treaty, which has resulted in the rehabilitation of the halibut industry on the Pacific coast. Encouraged by that, he devoted much time and effort for long years to arranging a treaty with the United States in connection with the Fraser river situation, and it was due to him more than to any other man, living or dead, that this was finally achieved.
Doctor Found was in office when many other reforms were carried out. I am speaking more of the Pacific coast, with which I am familiar. He was at the head of the branch at the time when the policy of breaking up the individual monopolistic control was carried out-the system under which one company absolutely controlled a large tract of water and no man could put hook, line or net in it without their consent. He was also responsible for initiating many of the regulations for the conservation of the salmon industry.
Some years ago the university of New Brunswick conferred on him the degree of Doctor of Science in recognition of his distinguished services. Doctor Found always had a strong sense of loyalty to the officials of his department, both those above him and those under him. Possibly at times he was subject to criticism in carrying out or defending, from a sense of loyalty, policies which he himself might not personally have approved. In that regard I have often strongly and perhaps violently opposed him in the carrying out of policies or in the method whereby he himself carried them out, but in the seventeen years that I have come in contact with him in his personal capacity I have never known him to say a discourteous word to anyone or to do a discreditable act. I am sure the wishes of all the members of this house who came in contact with him go out to him in his retirement, in the hope that he may for many years enjoy a well-earned rest.

Just a word on that. For the information of the hon. member, may I tell him that the gentleman to whom he has referred has been superannuated for cause at my own request, according to files that are
public. I will say no more now, but I regret very much that an example is not made of the wrongs done by former civil servants who have left the service for very good reasons. This is one instance in which I could say much more. I had the file for three months and I know something about the matter. I speak with knowledge, and I say that an example should be made of Mr. Found to indicate to the service that there should be no favouritism such as he has been guilty of. That is my point of view and I speak with knowledge. We have had enough of these compliments paid to unworthy civil servants.

It seems to me that
the Minister of Fisheries should say something after the remarks just made.
